hypotheses.title: Referral fee is computed but never paid to referrer
hypotheses.description: `referralFeeCost` is calculated as the portion of `buyerFeeTotal` owed to the referrer, but the function only transfers `baseAmount - sellerFeeTotal` to the seller and `buyerFeeTotal + sellerFeeTotal` to the fee collector. No transfer is ever made to `_referral`, so the referral reward is silently absorbed by the fee collector while the event reports it as paid to the referrer.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker (or any buyer) purchases with a valid `_referral` address. 2) `referralFeeCost` is computed and emitted in the `Purchased` event. 3) The full `buyerFeeTotal` is sent to `feeCollector`; the referrer receives nothing. 4) Off-chain accounting/events claim the referrer was paid, but on-chain balances show otherwise.
hypotheses.impact: Referrers are systematically underpaid; fee collector over-collects; event logs misreport fund flows, breaking integrator accounting.
hypotheses.recommendation: Transfer `referralFeeCost` to `_referral` (or to `referralFeeCollector`) and subtract it from `feeCollectorTotal` before sending to the fee collector.

hypotheses.title: Anyone can re-initialize Marketplace and VestingManager via proxy
hypotheses.description: `initialize` uses the `initializer` modifier from OpenZeppelin's `Initializable`, but the contract is deployed behind a proxy and the implementation contract itself is never initialized. An attacker can call `initialize` directly on the implementation contract (or on the proxy if the deployer forgot to initialize it) to set `marketplaceSetting` to an attacker-controlled address, then use that to bypass all admin checks that read `s2Admin()` from the setting contract.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker calls `initialize(attackerToken, attackerSetting)` on the uninitialized implementation/proxy. 2) Attacker deploys a fake `IMarketplaceSetting` returning attacker as `s2Admin`. 3) Attacker calls `addCoin`, `setMarketplaceSettingAddress`, or any admin-gated function and passes the check. 4) Attacker can also point `marketplaceSetting` to a malicious contract that returns arbitrary fees, penalty, and vestingManager, redirecting all funds.
hypotheses.impact: Full takeover of marketplace configuration: attacker can add arbitrary payment tokens, redirect fee collector, change vesting manager, and drain funds routed through the marketplace.
hypotheses.recommendation: Call `_disableInitializers()` in the constructor of every upgradeable contract and ensure the proxy is initialized atomically at deployment.

hypotheses.title: VestingManager.initialize callable by anyone on implementation
hypotheses.description: `SecondSwap_VestingManager` is upgradeable and its `initialize(address _s2admin)` is protected only by the `initializer` modifier. If the implementation contract (or an uninitialized proxy) is reachable, any external actor can call `initialize` and set themselves as `s2Admin`, gaining access to `setMarketplace`, `setAdmin`, `setBuyerFee`, `setSellerFee`, and `setVestingDeployer`.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker calls `initialize(attacker)` on the uninitialized implementation/proxy. 2) Attacker calls `setMarketplace(attackerControlled)` to become the marketplace. 3) Attacker calls `listVesting`/`completePurchase`/`unlistVesting` directly to move vesting tokens arbitrarily. 4) Attacker can also set fees to 5000 bps and redirect all fee flows.
hypotheses.impact: Complete control of vesting allocations and marketplace integration; attacker can mint/transfer vesting positions and steal tokens held by the manager.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add `_disableInitializers()` in the constructor and initialize the proxy in the same transaction as deployment.

hypotheses.title: transferVesting reduces releaseRate causing under-claim for grantor
hypotheses.description: When a grantor transfers part of their vesting, `grantorVesting.totalAmount` is reduced and `releaseRate` is recomputed as `totalAmount / numOfSteps`. However, `stepsClaimed` and `amountClaimed` are not adjusted. If the grantor had already claimed steps, the new `releaseRate` is applied to the remaining steps, but the already-claimed amount is not subtracted from the new total, so the grantor can end up with `amountClaimed > totalAmount` or, more commonly, the remaining claimable amount is understated because `releaseRate * (numOfSteps - stepsClaimed)` may be less than `totalAmount - amountClaimed`. The grantor loses vested tokens.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Grantor has a vesting with `totalAmount = 1000`, `numOfSteps = 10`, `releaseRate = 100`. 2) After 5 steps, grantor claims 500 (`amountClaimed = 500`, `stepsClaimed = 5`). 3) Grantor transfers 400 to a beneficiary. `totalAmount` becomes 600, `releaseRate = 600/10 = 60`. 4) Remaining claimable = `60 * 5 = 300`, but grantor should have `600 - 500 = 100` remaining. Actually grantor gets 300, which is more than 100 — but the beneficiary also gets 400 with `stepsClaimed = 5`, so beneficiary's `releaseRate = 400/(10-5) = 80`, claimable = `80*5 = 400`. Total claimed = 500 + 300 + 400 = 1200 > 1000. The contract is now insolvent by 200 tokens.
hypotheses.impact: Double-counting of vested tokens; contract becomes insolvent; later claimers cannot withdraw.
hypotheses.recommendation: When transferring, recompute `releaseRate` based on remaining unclaimed amount and remaining steps, and ensure `amountClaimed` is properly accounted for in both grantor and beneficiary vestings.

hypotheses.title: available() returns unvested total, allowing over-listing
hypotheses.description: `available()` returns `totalAmount - amountClaimed`, which is the entire remaining vesting allocation regardless of how many steps have actually vested. `SecondSwap_VestingManager.listVesting` uses this value to bound `amount`, so a seller can list (and transfer to the manager) tokens that have not yet vested. Combined with `transferVesting`'s check `totalAmount - amountClaimed >= _amount`, the seller can move unvested tokens into the marketplace, and buyers can purchase them, effectively unlocking tokens ahead of schedule.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Seller has a vesting schedule with most tokens unvested. 2) Seller calls `listVesting` with `amount` up to `available()` (full remaining total). 3) Manager transfers the unvested tokens to itself via `transferVesting`. 4) Buyers purchase and receive tokens that should still be locked.
hypotheses.impact: Vesting schedule is bypassed; unvested tokens are sold and delivered early, breaking the vesting guarantee and potentially draining the vesting contract's token balance.
hypotheses.recommendation: `available()` should return only the currently claimable amount (based on elapsed steps), not `totalAmount - amountClaimed`.

hypotheses.title: completePurchase transfers vesting with stepsClaimed=0, resetting buyer's schedule
hypotheses.description: `completePurchase` calls `SecondSwap_Vesting(vesting).transferVesting(address(this), buyer, amount)`. In `transferVesting`, the buyer's new vesting is created with `_stepsClaimed = grantorVesting.stepsClaimed` (the marketplace's stepsClaimed, which is 0 for the marketplace's aggregated vesting). This means the buyer receives a fresh vesting schedule starting from step 0, even though the tokens may have been partially vested already. The buyer can then claim tokens that were already vested at the time of purchase, effectively double-claiming against the original seller's schedule.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Seller lists 1000 tokens that are 50% vested (5/10 steps). 2) Buyer purchases 1000 tokens. 3) `completePurchase` transfers 1000 vesting to buyer with `stepsClaimed = 0`. 4) Buyer immediately calls `claim()` and receives 500 tokens (5 steps worth) that were already vested. 5) Seller already received payment for the full 1000. 6) The contract now owes 500 tokens to buyer that were already accounted for in the seller's original vesting, causing insolvency.
hypotheses.impact: Double-claiming of vested tokens; contract insolvency; later claimers cannot withdraw.
hypotheses.recommendation: When transferring vesting from the marketplace to a buyer, preserve the original `stepsClaimed` from the seller's vesting, or compute the correct `stepsClaimed` based on elapsed time.

hypotheses.title: transferVesting recomputes releaseRate ignoring already-claimed steps
hypotheses.description: `transferVesting` reduces `grantorVesting.totalAmount` and recomputes `releaseRate = totalAmount / numOfSteps`, but does not account for `stepsClaimed` or `amountClaimed`. If the grantor has already claimed some steps, the new releaseRate is too low relative to remaining steps, and the grantor's future `claimable` will under-pay. Conversely, `_createVesting` for the beneficiary uses `releaseRate = _totalAmount / (numOfSteps - _stepsClaimed)`, which is correct for the beneficiary. The asymmetry means the grantor's remaining vesting is silently reduced.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Grantor has 100 tokens over 10 steps, claims 5 steps (50 tokens, stepsClaimed=5, amountClaimed=50, totalAmount=100). 2) Grantor transfers 50 to beneficiary. 3) grantorVesting.totalAmount = 50, releaseRate = 50/10 = 5. 4) Grantor's remaining claimable = 5 * (10-5) = 25, but should be 50. Grantor loses 25 tokens of vesting.
hypotheses.impact: Loss of vested tokens for the grantor; incorrect accounting of remaining vesting.
hypotheses.recommendation: Recompute releaseRate as `(totalAmount - amountClaimed) / (numOfSteps - stepsClaimed)` in `transferVesting`, matching `_createVesting`'s logic.

hypotheses.title: referralFeeCost can exceed buyerFeeTotal causing feeCollector underpayment
hypotheses.description: `referralFeeCost = buyerFeeTotal - (baseAmount * bfee * referralFee) / (BASE * BASE)`. If `referralFee` is set high (up to 10000 = 100%) and `bfee` is high, the subtracted term can exceed `buyerFeeTotal`, causing underflow revert. Even when it doesn't revert, the feeCollector receives `buyerFeeTotal + sellerFeeTotal` but the referral is paid out of `buyerFeeTotal` implicitly — however, the code never actually transfers `referralFeeCost` to the referrer; it only emits it in the event. The referrer receives nothing, and the feeCollector receives the full buyerFeeTotal, so the referral reward is silently dropped.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Buyer purchases with a referral. 2) `referralFeeCost` is computed and emitted. 3) No transfer to `_referral` occurs. 4) Referrer gets nothing; feeCollector keeps all fees.
hypotheses.impact: Referrers never receive rewards despite event emission; accounting mismatch between emitted event and actual transfers.
hypotheses.recommendation: Actually transfer `referralFeeCost` to `_referral` (or `referralFeeCollector`) and subtract it from `feeCollectorTotal`.

hypotheses.title: unlistVesting subtracts full listing.balance even after partial sales
hypotheses.description: `unlistVesting` calls `IVestingManager.unlistVesting(listing.seller, _vestingPlan, listing.balance)` and then sets `listing.balance = 0`. However, `listing.balance` is the *remaining* amount, while the manager's `allocations[seller][plan].sold` was incremented by the *original* listed amount at list time and only decremented by `amount` on unlist. After partial sales, `listing.balance < original listed amount`, so the manager's `sold` counter is decremented by less than it was incremented, leaving a residual `sold` value that permanently reduces the seller's future sell limit.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Seller lists 1000 tokens (manager `sold += 1000`). 2) Buyer purchases 400 (listing.balance = 600). 3) Seller unlists; manager `sold -= 600`, leaving `sold = 400` even though the seller no longer has any listed tokens. 4) Seller's future `listVesting` calls are capped by the phantom `sold = 400`, blocking legitimate listings.
hypotheses.impact: Sellers permanently lose sell capacity; `allocations.sold` drifts from reality, causing denial of future listings and incorrect max-sell-percent accounting.
hypotheses.recommendation: On unlist, decrement `allocations[seller][plan].sold` by the original listed amount minus already-sold amount, or track listed amount separately from remaining balance.

hypotheses.title: unlistVesting refunds full balance without checking buyer purchases
hypotheses.description: `unlistVesting` sets `listing.balance = 0` and calls `IVestingManager.unlistVesting(listing.seller, _vestingPlan, listing.balance)` — but `listing.balance` was just zeroed, so the manager is asked to return 0 tokens. Meanwhile the seller's `allocations[seller][plan].sold` was incremented at list time and is only decremented by the amount passed (0), leaving the seller's sold counter permanently inflated. The seller can then re-list the same vesting again, and the manager's `sellLimit` check is bypassed because `sold` was never reduced.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Seller lists `amount` tokens; manager increments `allocations[seller][plan].sold += amount` and transfers vesting to manager. 2) Seller calls `unlistVesting`. 3) `listing.balance` is set to 0 before the manager call, so `unlistVesting(seller, plan, 0)` decrements `sold` by 0 and transfers 0 tokens back. 4) Seller's vesting remains in the manager, but `sold` is still `amount`. 5) Seller re-lists the same tokens; `sellLimit` is computed from `bought` and `sold`, and since `sold` is already inflated, the check may pass or fail inconsistently, but the seller can also call `unlistVesting` repeatedly to manipulate `sold` accounting.
hypotheses.impact: Seller's `sold` counter is corrupted; tokens can be locked in the manager or the seller can bypass max-sell-percent limits, leading to over-selling and potential insolvency of the vesting pool.
hypotheses.recommendation: Capture `listing.balance` into a local variable before zeroing it, and pass that value to `IVestingManager.unlistVesting`.

hypotheses.title: available() returns total minus claimed, ignoring step schedule
hypotheses.description: `available()` returns `totalAmount - amountClaimed`, which is the entire remaining vesting regardless of how many steps have elapsed. The VestingManager uses `available()` in `listVesting` to check the seller has enough tokens to list. A seller can list tokens that are not yet vested (future steps), effectively selling unvested tokens. If the seller later claims before the buyer, or if the vesting is transferred, the buyer may receive tokens that are not yet unlocked, or the contract may be unable to honor both claims.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Seller has 1000 tokens vesting over 10 steps, 0 steps elapsed. 2) `available()` returns 1000. 3) Seller lists 1000 tokens on the marketplace. 4) Buyer purchases; `completePurchase` transfers 1000 vesting to buyer. 5) Seller's vesting is now 0, buyer's vesting is 1000 with `stepsClaimed = 0`. 6) Buyer can only claim as steps elapse, but the seller already received payment for tokens that were never unlocked. If the token issuer revokes or the vesting is slashed, buyer loses.
hypotheses.impact: Buyers can purchase unvested tokens; if the underlying vesting is subject to revocation or the token issuer does not fund the contract, buyers suffer losses.
hypotheses.recommendation: `available()` should return only the currently claimable amount (based on elapsed steps), or `listVesting` should use `claimable()` instead.

hypotheses.title: LINEAR discount uses current balance, enabling self-referential price manipulation
hypotheses.description: For `DiscountType.LINEAR`, the discount is `(_amount * discountPct) / listing.total`, but `_amount` is the buyer-supplied purchase size and `listing.total` is fixed. A buyer can choose `_amount` to maximize the discount, and because `_validatePurchase` allows `_amount == listing.balance` for PARTIAL listings, a buyer can sweep the entire remaining balance at the maximum discount. There is no minimum-out check, so the buyer effectively sets their own price.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker observes a LINEAR listing with `discountPct` near 10000. 2) Attacker calls `spotPurchase` with `_amount = listing.balance` (allowed by `_amount == listing.balance` branch). 3) Discount approaches `discountPct`, so attacker pays near-zero for the full remaining balance. 4) Seller receives almost nothing.
hypotheses.impact: Seller receives far less than intended; buyer acquires vested tokens at near-zero cost.
hypotheses.recommendation: Cap the LINEAR discount by a per-listing maximum, or compute the discount against a fixed reference (e.g., `listing.total` at listing time) and require a minimum effective price.

hypotheses.title: Reentrancy in spotPurchase via malicious payment token
hypotheses.description: In `spotPurchase`, `_handleTransfers` performs `safeTransferFrom`/`safeTransfer` on `listing.currency` (an arbitrary admin-supported token) BEFORE `listing.balance` and `listing.status` are updated. If the currency token has a callback (ERC-777, ERC-20 with hooks, or a malicious token added via `addCoin`), the recipient (seller, feeCollector, or the token itself) can reenter `spotPurchase` and purchase again against the stale `listing.balance`, draining the listing beyond its intended amount.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker lists a vesting with a hook-capable currency token (or gets such a token added). 2) Attacker (as buyer) calls `spotPurchase`; during `safeTransfer`/`safeTransferFrom` the token invokes a callback into `spotPurchase` again. 3) Because `listing.balance` is still the pre-purchase value, the reentrant call passes `_validatePurchase` and repeats transfers. 4) Repeat until listing balance is exhausted or vesting manager reverts, but payment already moved.
hypotheses.impact: Buyer can purchase more tokens than the listing balance, causing accounting corruption in `allocations` and draining the vesting plan's tokens; seller/feeCollector may receive duplicated payments or the marketplace may become insolvent.
hypotheses.recommendation: Apply checks-effects-interactions: decrement `listing.balance` and update `listing.status` before `_handleTransfers`, and/or add a nonReentrant guard on `spotPurchase`.

hypotheses.title: Referral fee paid from buyer fee without reducing feeCollector share
hypotheses.description: `referralFeeCost` is computed as a portion of `buyerFeeTotal`, but the full `buyerFeeTotal + sellerFeeTotal` is still transferred to `feeCollector`. The referral reward is never actually deducted from the feeCollector's share nor transferred to the referrer in this function. The event reports a referral reward that is never paid, and the referrer receives nothing while the feeCollector is overpaid relative to the intended split.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker (buyer) supplies a `_referral` address they control. 2) `_handleTransfers` computes `referralFeeCost > 0` and emits it in the `Purchased` event. 3) No transfer to `_referral` occurs; the entire fee goes to `feeCollector`. 4) Off-chain accounting based on the event credits the referrer, but on-chain no funds move, causing a mismatch that can be exploited in any downstream reward distribution that trusts the event.
hypotheses.impact: Referrers are never paid; feeCollector receives more than intended; off-chain reward systems relying on the event can be drained or mis-accounted.
hypotheses.recommendation: Deduct `referralFeeCost` from `feeCollectorTotal` and transfer it to `_referral` (or to `referralFeeCollector`) before sending the remainder to `feeCollector`.

hypotheses.title: LINEAR discount can be gamed by splitting purchases
hypotheses.description: For `DiscountType.LINEAR`, the discount is `pricePerUnit * (BASE - (_amount * discountPct / listing.total)) / BASE`. Because `_amount` is the current purchase size, a buyer who splits a large purchase into many small ones pays a higher per-unit price, but a buyer who buys the entire remaining balance in one call gets the maximum discount. Conversely, a buyer can front-run other buyers by purchasing a large chunk first to lock in a deep discount, then resell or hold, while later buyers pay full price. The discount is not tied to any time or commitment, so it is purely a function of purchase size and can be exploited by timing.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker observes a listing with LINEAR discount. 2) Attacker buys the largest possible `_amount` in a single transaction to obtain the maximum discount (up to `discountPct`). 3) Attacker immediately resells the purchased vesting on the same marketplace (or another) at the undiscounted price, capturing the spread. 4) Alternatively, attacker splits purchases to avoid triggering the discount for competitors while still acquiring tokens cheaply.
hypotheses.impact: Value extraction from sellers and other buyers; sellers receive less than intended; discount mechanism is not economically sound.
hypotheses.recommendation: Base the discount on cumulative purchased amount per buyer, or apply a time-weighted/commitment-based discount rather than instantaneous purchase size.

hypotheses.title: _getDiscountedPrice LINEAR discount can exceed 100% for large amounts
hypotheses.description: For LINEAR discount, `discountedPrice = pricePerUnit * (BASE - (_amount * discountPct / total)) / BASE`. If `_amount == total` and `discountPct == BASE` (10000), the factor is 0, which is fine. But `discountPct` is not bounded to <= BASE in `listVesting`; only `_discountPct > 0` is required. A seller can set `discountPct > 10000`, making `BASE - (...)` underflow and revert, or with `_amount * discountPct / total > BASE`, the subtraction underflows. This causes purchases to revert (DoS) for listings with high discountPct.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Seller lists with `discountType = LINEAR`, `discountPct = 20000`. 2) Buyer attempts purchase with `_amount` such that `_amount * 20000 / total > 10000`. 3) Subtraction underflows, transaction reverts. Buyer cannot purchase.
hypotheses.impact: DoS on purchases for listings with discountPct > BASE; seller can grief buyers or lock listing.
hypotheses.recommendation: In `listVesting`, require `_discountPct <= BASE` when `_discountType != NO`.

hypotheses.title: LINEAR discount uses full listing total, not remaining balance
hypotheses.description: For `DiscountType.LINEAR`, the discount is computed as `_amount * discountPct / listing.total`, where `listing.total` is the original listed amount, not the current `listing.balance`. As purchases deplete the listing, the same `_amount` yields a smaller discount fraction than intended, and the last buyer of a nearly-empty listing pays almost full price even though the discount was meant to scale with purchase size relative to the listing.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Seller lists with LINEAR discount. 2) Early buyers purchase large chunks, shrinking `balance`. 3) A later buyer purchasing the remaining balance receives a discount computed against the original `total`, not the remaining amount, so the effective discount is diluted. 4) Buyer pays more than the linear schedule implies; seller/fee collector capture the difference.
hypotheses.impact: Buyers overpay relative to the advertised linear discount schedule; pricing is inconsistent across the listing lifetime.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use `listing.balance` (or the pre-purchase remaining amount) as the denominator for the linear discount calculation.

hypotheses.title: _createVesting addition path ignores stepsClaimed in releaseRate
hypotheses.description: When adding to an existing vesting, `releaseRate` is set to `(totalAmount - amountClaimed) / (numOfSteps - stepsClaimed)`. If `stepsClaimed == numOfSteps` (fully claimed schedule) the else-branch sets `releaseRate = 0`, but `totalAmount` is still incremented. The newly added amount becomes permanently unclaimable because `claimable()` returns `totalAmount - amountClaimed` only when `stepsClaimed + claimableSteps >= numOfSteps`, and `claimableSteps` will be 0 once all steps are consumed.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Beneficiary fully claims all steps. 2) An authorized caller adds more vesting via `createVesting`/`createVestings`. 3) `releaseRate` becomes 0 and `stepsClaimed == numOfSteps`, so `claimable()` returns 0 forever. 4) Added tokens are locked in the contract.
hypotheses.impact: Newly added vesting amounts are permanently frozen; tokens are stuck in the vesting contract with no path to the beneficiary.
hypotheses.recommendation: When `stepsClaimed >= numOfSteps`, either revert on additional vesting or reset `stepsClaimed`/recompute schedule so the new amount is claimable.

hypotheses.title: Missing slippage/min-out protection in spotPurchase allows price manipulation
hypotheses.description: `spotPurchase` computes the payment amount from `listing.pricePerUnit` and the discount, but never accepts a `minAmountOut`/`maxAmountIn` parameter from the buyer. The buyer has no way to bound the price they pay, so any change to the effective price (e.g., via the LINEAR discount which depends on `_amount` and `listing.total`, or via a seller re-listing) is silently accepted. Because the discount formula `(_amount * discountPct) / listing.total` is computed on the fly, a buyer cannot predict or protect against the final price.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker (seller) creates a listing with `DiscountType.LINEAR` and a large `discountPct`. 2) Buyer submits `spotPurchase` expecting a certain price. 3) Seller front-runs by adjusting listing parameters (or the buyer's `_amount` interacts with `listing.total` differently than expected), causing the buyer to pay more than intended with no revert. 4) Buyer's funds are drained at an unfavorable rate.
hypotheses.impact: Buyer overpays for vested tokens; loss of funds with no on-chain protection.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add `minAmountOut`/`maxAmountIn` parameters to `spotPurchase` and require the computed `baseAmount + buyerFeeTotal` to satisfy them.

hypotheses.title: Rounding in baseAmount lets buyer pay zero for small purchases
hypotheses.description: `baseAmount = (_amount * discountedPrice) / 10**decimals`. If `_amount * discountedPrice < 10**decimals`, `baseAmount` truncates to 0, and the only guard is `require(baseAmount > 0)`. However, a buyer can pick `_amount` such that `baseAmount` is 1 wei while `_amount` is large (e.g., when `discountedPrice` is tiny due to a large LINEAR discount). The buyer then pays 1 wei of currency for a large amount of vested tokens.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker finds a listing with a small `pricePerUnit` and a large `discountPct`. 2) Attacker computes `_amount` such that `_amount * discountedPrice` is just above `10**decimals`. 3) Attacker calls `spotPurchase` and pays ~1 wei for a large token amount. 4) `completePurchase` transfers the full `_amount` of vesting to the attacker.
hypotheses.impact: Buyer drains the listing for negligible payment; seller loses vested tokens.
hypotheses.recommendation: Enforce a minimum `baseAmount` proportional to `_amount` (e.g., `baseAmount >= _amount * minPricePerUnit / 10**decimals`), or reject purchases where the effective price per unit falls below a floor.

hypotheses.title: Cross-function reentrancy between spotPurchase and unlistVesting
hypotheses.description: `spotPurchase` updates `listing.balance`/`status` only after `_handleTransfers` completes, and `unlistVesting` also performs external calls before state updates. A malicious currency token callback during `spotPurchase` can invoke `unlistVesting` (or vice versa) while the listing state is stale, allowing the same listing to be both purchased and unlisted in the same transaction.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker lists tokens with a hook-capable currency. 2) Attacker calls `spotPurchase`; during the token transfer callback, attacker calls `unlistVesting` on the same listing. 3) `unlistVesting` sees `status == LIST` and returns `listing.balance` tokens to the seller via the vesting manager. 4) Control returns to `spotPurchase`, which then decrements `listing.balance` and calls `completePurchase`, transferring tokens to the buyer as well.
hypotheses.impact: The same listed tokens are delivered to both the seller (via unlist) and the buyer (via completePurchase), draining the vesting manager's pooled tokens and corrupting `allocations` for both parties.
hypotheses.recommendation: Enforce checks-effects-interactions in both functions and add a shared `nonReentrant` guard covering all state-mutating marketplace entry points.

hypotheses.title: transferVesting allows replay of vesting claims via stepsClaimed copy
hypotheses.description: When a grantor transfers vesting to a beneficiary, `_createVesting` is called with `grantorVesting.stepsClaimed` as the new beneficiary's `stepsClaimed`. This means the beneficiary inherits the grantor's already-claimed step count, but the grantor's `amountClaimed` is not transferred. The grantor's `releaseRate` is recomputed as `totalAmount / numOfSteps` (not `(totalAmount - amountClaimed) / (numOfSteps - stepsClaimed)`), so the grantor can continue claiming steps that were already claimed before the transfer, effectively double-claiming tokens from the same vesting schedule.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker is a grantor with a vesting schedule. 2) Attacker claims some steps, accumulating `amountClaimed` and `stepsClaimed`. 3) Attacker calls `transferVesting` (via manager/deployer path) to move remaining tokens to a fresh beneficiary address they control. 4) The new beneficiary inherits `stepsClaimed` but `amountClaimed=0`, so `claimable()` returns `totalAmount - 0` once enough steps pass. 5) Attacker claims the full amount on the new address while the original grantor's `releaseRate` was reset to `totalAmount/numOfSteps`, allowing further claims on the original address too.
hypotheses.impact: Double-claiming of vested tokens; the vesting contract's token balance is drained beyond the intended allocation, causing insolvency for other beneficiaries.
hypotheses.recommendation: When transferring vesting, compute the new beneficiary's `releaseRate` from `(totalAmount - amountClaimed) / (numOfSteps - stepsClaimed)` and reset the grantor's `amountClaimed`/`stepsClaimed` consistently, or disallow transfers after any claim.

hypotheses.title: unlistVesting penalty uses USDT balance check but transfers from seller without approval
hypotheses.description: The penalty check requires `usdt.balanceOf(msg.sender) >= penaltyFee`, but the actual transfer uses `safeTransferFrom(msg.sender, feeCollector, penaltyFee)`. If the seller has not approved the marketplace for USDT, the transfer reverts, preventing unlisting. A seller who wants to unlist but has no USDT approval is stuck. Additionally, the balance check is on `usdt` but the listing currency may be different, so a seller with sufficient listing currency but no USDT cannot unlist.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Seller lists tokens. 2) Seller wants to unlist before `minListingDuration` expires. 3) Seller has USDT balance but has not approved the marketplace. 4) `safeTransferFrom` reverts, unlisting fails. 5) Seller's tokens remain locked in the marketplace until duration expires.
hypotheses.impact: Sellers cannot unlist early even if they have the penalty fee; tokens are locked longer than necessary; potential DoS on unlisting.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use `safeTransferFrom` with a prior `approve` check, or allow the penalty to be paid in the listing currency, or use `transferFrom` with a fallback.

hypotheses.title: Marketplace listing transfers vesting to manager but unlist uses wrong seller
hypotheses.description: When a listing is created, `listVesting` calls `IVestingManager.listVesting(msg.sender, ...)` which transfers the vesting from the seller to the manager contract. On unlist, the marketplace calls `IVestingManager.unlistVesting(listing.seller, _vestingPlan, listing.balance)`, which internally does `transferVesting(address(this), seller, amount)`. However, if the admin (not the seller) calls `unlistVesting`, the vesting is still returned to `listing.seller`, which is correct, but the penalty fee is skipped for admin. The real inconsistency: `listing.balance` is used as the amount to unlist, but the manager's `allocations[seller][plan].sold` was incremented by the full listed amount at list time and never decremented for partial sales. After a partial purchase, `listing.balance` is less than the original listed amount, so unlisting returns only the remaining balance while `allocations[seller][plan].sold` is decremented by that smaller amount, leaving `sold` inflated. This corrupts the seller's sell-limit accounting, allowing them to list more than `maxSellPercent` in subsequent listings.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Seller lists 100 tokens (sold += 100). 2) Buyer purchases 50 (balance = 50, sold still 100). 3) Seller unlists: manager does `sold -= 50` → sold = 50, but seller only ever sold 50 net. 4) Seller can now list again; sellLimit computation uses inflated `sold` history inconsistently, letting them exceed maxSellPercent across cycles.
hypotheses.impact: Wrong accounting of `allocations[seller][plan].sold` allows sellers to bypass `maxSellPercent` limits, potentially dumping more vesting than permitted and breaking the sell-limit invariant.
hypotheses.recommendation: In `unlistVesting`, decrement `allocations[seller][plan].sold` by the original listed amount (or track remaining listed amount separately), not by `listing.balance`.

hypotheses.title: setTokenOwner mapping keyed by owner allows overwriting token ownership
hypotheses.description: `_tokenOwner` is keyed by owner address, not token address. The check `require(_tokenOwner[_owner] == address(0))` only prevents setting an owner that already has a token. But an admin can set the same token to multiple owners (since the mapping is owner→token), and more importantly, `deployVesting` checks `_tokenOwner[msg.sender] == tokenAddress`. If admin sets `_tokenOwner[attacker] = tokenA`, the attacker can deploy vestings for tokenA. The mapping direction is inverted from the natural token→owner, allowing one token to be associated with multiple owners and enabling unauthorized vesting creation.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Admin sets `_tokenOwner[alice] = tokenA`. 2) Admin later sets `_tokenOwner[bob] = tokenA` (allowed since `_tokenOwner[bob] == 0`). 3) Both alice and bob can now deploy vestings for tokenA, doubling issuance authority.
hypotheses.impact: Multiple addresses can create vestings for the same token, breaking token issuance control and potentially minting/allocating more vesting than intended.
hypotheses.recommendation: Key `_tokenOwner` by token address (`mapping(address => address)`) and check `_tokenOwner[tokenAddress] == msg.sender`.

hypotheses.title: transferVesting in StepVesting callable by vestingDeployer set at construction
hypotheses.description: `transferVesting` allows `msg.sender == vestingDeployer` to move any grantor's vesting to any beneficiary. `vestingDeployer` is set in the constructor to the deployer contract address, but the deployer contract's `transferVesting` only checks `_tokenOwner[msg.sender] == token`. If an attacker can become the token owner via `setTokenOwner` (see initializer finding) or if the deployer is ever replaced, they can arbitrarily move any user's vesting. Additionally, the check `grantorVesting.totalAmount - grantorVesting.amountClaimed >= _amount` does not prevent transferring already-claimed steps to a new beneficiary with `_stepsClaimed` set, effectively duplicating claim rights.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker obtains token-owner status (via initializer takeover or admin misconfiguration). 2) Attacker calls `SecondSwap_VestingDeployer.transferVesting(victim, attacker, amount, stepVesting, "")`. 3) Deployer forwards to `StepVesting.transferVesting` which passes the `vestingDeployer` check. 4) Attacker receives a fresh vesting with `_stepsClaimed` copied from victim, allowing them to claim future steps that victim already partially claimed.
hypotheses.impact: Theft of vesting allocations; double-claiming of steps; accounting corruption in `_vestings`.
hypotheses.recommendation: Restrict `transferVesting` to `manager` only, or require explicit grantor authorization; also verify `_stepsClaimed` semantics when transferring.

hypotheses.title: No oracle/price feed validation; pricePerUnit is fully seller-controlled
hypotheses.description: `listVesting` accepts an arbitrary `_price` from the seller with only `require(_price > 0)`. There is no oracle, TWAP, or sanity check against a reference price. A seller can list at an absurdly high price, and a buyer (or a bot) that trusts the listing without an external check will overpay. Conversely, a seller can list at a near-zero price to grief other sellers or to wash-trade.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker (seller) lists vested tokens at `_price = 1` wei per unit. 2) An unsuspecting buyer or an automated buyer that does not independently verify price calls `spotPurchase`. 3) Buyer pays a trivial amount, but the seller's intent (e.g., to manipulate a downstream accounting system that reads `pricePerUnit`) is achieved. 4) Alternatively, a seller lists at an extreme high price and a naive buyer overpays.
hypotheses.impact: Buyers can be tricked into overpaying; downstream systems relying on `pricePerUnit` get manipulated values.
hypotheses.recommendation: Integrate a price oracle (e.g., Chainlink) or a TWAP and require `_price` to be within a sane band of the reference price.

hypotheses.title: Discount applied before fee, but fee base uses discounted amount — fee manipulation
hypotheses.description: `buyerFeeTotal = (baseAmount * bfee) / BASE` and `sellerFeeTotal = (baseAmount * sfee) / BASE` are computed on the discounted `baseAmount`. A buyer who maximizes the discount (via LINEAR) also minimizes the fees paid to the protocol and seller. There is no minimum fee floor, so a buyer can structure `_amount` to make `baseAmount` tiny and pay near-zero fees.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker picks `_amount` to maximize the LINEAR discount. 2) `baseAmount` becomes very small. 3) `buyerFeeTotal` and `sellerFeeTotal` become ~0. 4) Protocol and seller receive almost no fees.
hypotheses.impact: Protocol revenue loss; seller receives less than expected.
hypotheses.recommendation: Compute fees on the pre-discount amount, or enforce a minimum fee floor.

hypotheses.title: Reentrancy in unlistVesting via penalty token transfer
hypotheses.description: `unlistVesting` calls `usdt.safeTransferFrom(msg.sender, feeCollector, penaltyFee)` before calling `IVestingManager.unlistVesting` and before setting `listing.status = DELIST` / `listing.balance = 0`. If `usdt` is a hook-capable token (or the feeCollector is a contract that reenters), the attacker can reenter `unlistVesting` while the listing is still `LIST`, causing the vesting manager to be invoked multiple times for the same listing.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker creates a listing with a hook-capable USDT-like token. 2) Attacker calls `unlistVesting`; during `safeTransferFrom` the token/feeCollector reenters `unlistVesting`. 3) The reentrant call sees `status == LIST` and calls `IVestingManager.unlistVesting` again, transferring `listing.balance` back to the seller multiple times.
hypotheses.impact: Seller can extract more tokens from the vesting manager than they listed, draining other users' allocations held by the manager; marketplace accounting (`allocations[seller][plan].sold`) is corrupted.
hypotheses.recommendation: Set `listing.status = DELIST` and `listing.balance = 0` before the external `safeTransferFrom` and `IVestingManager.unlistVesting` calls, or add a reentrancy guard.

hypotheses.title: Early-unlist penalty blocks admin from unlisting but also blocks seller when out of USDT
hypotheses.description: If a seller lists and then within `minListingDuration` wants to delist, they must hold `penaltyFee` USDT and approve the marketplace; otherwise `safeTransferFrom` reverts. Combined with the fact that delisting is the only exit, a seller without USDT balance or approval cannot recover their vested tokens for the entire `minListingDuration` window. Worse, the admin must call `unlistVesting` themselves to bypass the fee, but the check `msg.sender != s2Admin` is the only bypass, and the tokens are returned to `listing.seller` regardless.
hypotheses.attackPath: Seller lists tokens; loses USDT or revokes approval. Cannot unlist until `minListingDuration` passes. Meanwhile the listing can be bought by anyone, draining the seller's position at the listed price with no recourse.
hypotheses.impact: Seller's tokens are locked and enforceable for sale against their will for the duration.
hypotheses.recommendation: Allow delisting by paying penalty in the listed currency or escrowed at listing time, or extend admin bypass deadline handling.

hypotheses.title: listVesting sellLimit uses stale bought/sold causing over-sell
hypotheses.description: The `sellLimit` computation uses `userAllocation.bought` and `userAllocation.sold` before incrementing `sold`, and the `currentAlloc + userAllocation.sold > userAllocation.bought` branch adds a percentage of the excess. Because `sold` is incremented after the check and `bought` is only updated on purchases, a seller who has bought tokens and then sells them can repeatedly list up to `maxSellPercent` of the excess each time, effectively selling more than the intended cap. The check `userAllocation.sold <= sellLimit` is performed after `sold += amount`, but `sellLimit` was computed with the pre-increment `sold`, so the comparison is off by `amount`.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker buys a small amount to set `bought`. 2) Attacker lists the maximum allowed by `sellLimit`. 3) Attacker unlists (which decrements `sold` by the passed amount, but as noted in the unlist bug, may decrement by 0). 4) Attacker re-lists, and because `sold` was not properly decremented, the `sellLimit` check passes again. 5) Attacker repeats to sell more than `maxSellPercent` of their allocation.
hypotheses.impact: Sellers can exceed the max-sell-percent cap, dumping more vesting tokens than allowed and potentially crashing the token price or draining the vesting pool.
hypotheses.recommendation: Compute `sellLimit` using the post-increment `sold` value, and ensure `unlistVesting` correctly decrements `sold` by the actual returned amount.

hypotheses.title: setMaxSellPercent callable by any tokenIssuer of a vesting plan
hypotheses.description: `setMaxSellPercent` only checks `SecondSwap_StepVesting(vesting).tokenIssuer() == msg.sender`. The `tokenIssuer` is set at construction to `msg.sender` of `deployVesting`, which is the caller of the deployer contract. Any address that deploys a vesting plan becomes its `tokenIssuer` and can set `maxSellPercent` to any value (including >10000), bypassing the intended cap and allowing sellers to list more than the configured percentage.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker deploys a vesting plan via `SecondSwap_VestingDeployer.deployVesting` (requires token ownership, but attacker can register their own token via `setTokenOwner` if they are admin — or use any token they own). 2) Attacker calls `setMaxSellPercent(vesting, type(uint256).max)`. 3) Sellers on that plan can now list unlimited amounts, breaking the sell-limit invariant enforced in `listVesting`.
hypotheses.impact: Sell-limit invariant broken; sellers can dump more than intended, potentially draining the vesting pool and harming buyers.
hypotheses.recommendation: Cap `maxSellPercent` to `BASE` (10000) and/or restrict the setter to `s2Admin`.

hypotheses.title: Stale/zero price not checked when listing is created or purchased
hypotheses.description: `spotPurchase` reads `listing.pricePerUnit` directly from storage without any freshness check. If a listing was created long ago and the underlying token's market price has moved, the buyer pays the stale price. There is also no check that `listing.pricePerUnit` is non-zero at purchase time (only at listing time), so if a listing is somehow created with a zero price via a future upgrade or a bug, `baseAmount` becomes 0 and the `require(baseAmount > 0)` reverts — but a buyer cannot recover.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker waits for a listing to become stale (price moved significantly). 2) Attacker calls `spotPurchase` at the stale price, either overpaying or underpaying depending on direction. 3) No revert occurs because there is no freshness check.
hypotheses.impact: Buyer or seller suffers economic loss due to stale pricing; no on-chain protection.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add a `maxPriceAge` check or require the seller to refresh the listing price periodically; also re-validate `pricePerUnit > 0` in `spotPurchase`.

hypotheses.title: Read-only reentrancy in claimable/available during claim
hypotheses.description: `claim()` updates `vesting.stepsClaimed` and `vesting.amountClaimed` before `token.safeTransfer`, but `available()` and `claimable()` are view functions that read `_vestings` state. If the vested token has a callback (ERC-777), an external contract invoked during `safeTransfer` can call `available()`/`claimable()` and observe the already-updated state, or conversely, a reentrant `claim()` from the token callback can be attempted. More critically, `transferVesting` (callable by manager/marketplace) can be reentered during the token transfer to move vesting out while `claim` is mid-flight.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker is a beneficiary whose vested token is hook-capable. 2) Attacker calls `claim()`; during `safeTransfer` the token invokes a callback into `transferVesting` (via a manager/marketplace path) or into another `claim()`. 3) Because `stepsClaimed`/`amountClaimed` were already incremented, a second `claim()` returns 0, but `transferVesting` can still move the remaining `totalAmount` out, leaving the contract's token balance short.
hypotheses.impact: Token balance of the vesting contract can be drained below the sum of outstanding `totalAmount - amountClaimed`, causing later claims to revert (frozen funds) and breaking the invariant that the contract holds enough tokens for all vestings.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add a `nonReentrant` guard to `claim`, `transferVesting`, and `_createVesting`, and ensure the contract's token balance invariant is checked after external transfers.

hypotheses.title: Freeze prevents sellers from unlisting and buyers from purchasing
hypotheses.description: The `isFreeze` modifier blocks both `unlistVesting` and `spotPurchase`. When admin freezes the marketplace, sellers cannot unlist their tokens and buyers cannot purchase. Tokens already transferred into the marketplace via `listVesting` become stuck indefinitely with no recovery path available during freeze.
hypotheses.attackPath: Admin sets frozen (trusted action), but even without that — the design flaw means if any unlisting reverts due to external dependency (e.g., `transferVesting` failing on the VestingManager), tokens are permanently trapped since the only exit path is `unlistVesting`. Note: freeze itself is a trusted path, but the concern is that the seller had no escape hatch if a single sub-call reverts — there is no fallback path.
hypotheses.impact: Seller's vested tokens sit in the marketplace/manager with no way to retrieve them; funds effectively frozen.
hypotheses.recommendation: Provide an emergency unlist path that is not gated by `isFreeze`, or allow delisting during freeze with a penalty.

hypotheses.title: Unlist reverts after partial sale due to balance mismatch
hypotheses.description: `listVesting` transferred the full `_amount` from seller to VestingManager. After partial `spotPurchase`, `listing.balance` is reduced, but the VestingManager still holds the unsold portion plus the transferred-out amount. `unlistVesting` calls `IVestingManager.unlistVesting(listing.seller, _vestingPlan, listing.balance)` — this is correct in principle, but the VestingManager's `allocations[seller][plan].sold` was decremented by the full original list amount on list, and only reduced by `completePurchase`'s bought on the buyer side. The seller's `sold` counter is reduced by `listing.balance` (unsold), so `sold` accounting reflects only sold portion. However, if the listing was created with SINGLE type and partially bought (not possible since SINGLE requires full), or if purchase amounts accumulate imprecisely, the `transferVesting` from manager back to seller may revert due to insufficient claimable/total in the seller's `_vestings` entry.
hypotheses.attackPath: Buyer purchases a large fraction of a PARTIAL listing. VestingManager `transferVesting` on purchase modifies the seller's `totalAmount` by subtracting `_amount` and recomputing `releaseRate = total/numOfSteps` (rounded down). If the seller's original total was already reduced and re-rounded on listing, subsequent unlist's `transferVesting(seller, amount)` can hit `insufficient balance` due to rounding drift across multiple transfers, bricking delisting.
hypotheses.impact: Seller cannot unlist the remaining balance; tokens are frozen in the manager.
hypotheses.recommendation: Track exact listed balance in VestingManager and use it directly instead of relying on `totalAmount - amountClaimed` comparisons that suffer rounding drift.

hypotheses.title: transferVesting in StepVesting can brick on rounding when transfer amount large
hypotheses.description: After `grantorVesting.totalAmount -= _amount`, `releaseRate = grantorVesting.totalAmount / numOfSteps` truncates. If `_amount` was small relative to total and steps are many, `releaseRate` can drop to 0 even when grantor still has `totalAmount - amountClaimed > 0`. Subsequent `claimable` returns 0 for all remaining steps (unless eventual `stepsClaimed + claimableSteps >= numOfSteps` shortcut triggers). More critically, when the manager transfers out from itself (`unlistVesting`), `grantorVesting` is the manager's vesting entry built from the remaining unlist amount; repeated buys/sells via transferVesting recompute releaseRate each time and can zero out claimable tokens.
hypotheses.attackPath: A buyer repeatedly buys small fractions of a listing, each triggering `transferVesting(manager, buyer, small)` and `transferVesting(seller, manager, amount)` — the seller's releaseRate is recomputed each time and truncation accumulates, eventually making the seller's remaining vesting unclaimable.
hypotheses.impact: Seller loses access to remaining unclaimed vesting tokens (they remain in struct but `claimable` returns 0 in edge cases).
hypotheses.recommendation: Track vesting via amounts, not recomputed releaseRate; or use a scaled precision factor (e.g., 1e18) when recomputing releaseRate.

hypotheses.title: Marketplace purchase has no deadline/nonce; signed intent replayable
hypotheses.description: `spotPurchase` executes purely on `msg.sender` with no signed authorization, nonce, deadline, or chain-id binding. Any meta-transaction or off-chain signed order that a relayer might submit on behalf of a buyer can be replayed by anyone on any chain where the marketplace is deployed, since the listing state is the only guard. Once a listing is partially filled, the same calldata can be re-submitted by any address that has approved the marketplace, draining the buyer's allowance repeatedly.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Buyer signs/approves an off-chain order for a partial purchase. 2) A relayer submits `spotPurchase` on the buyer's behalf. 3) An attacker observes the calldata and re-submits the identical call (same `_vestingPlan`, `_listingId`, `_amount`, `_referral`) from the buyer's account via a meta-tx relayer or by front-running with the buyer's still-valid allowance. 4) Because there is no nonce/deadline, the call succeeds again as long as the listing still has balance and the buyer's allowance remains.
hypotheses.impact: Buyer's payment tokens are spent multiple times for the same intended order; buyer loses funds and receives duplicate vesting allocations.
hypotheses.recommendation: Introduce an EIP-712 signed order with nonce, deadline, chainId, and verifyingContract, and consume the nonce on execution.

hypotheses.title: unlistVesting lets admin bypass penalty and drain seller vesting
hypotheses.description: `unlistVesting` allows `s2Admin` to unlist any seller's listing without paying the penalty fee and without the seller's consent. The admin path skips the penalty branch entirely and calls `IVestingManager.unlistVesting(listing.seller, ...)`, returning the seller's tokens to the seller — but the admin can also front-run or grief by unlisting at will. More critically, the admin can unlist a listing that a buyer is about to purchase, and combined with `setMarketplaceSettingAddress` (also admin-only) the admin can redirect `vestingManager` to a malicious contract that misroutes the returned tokens.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Admin (or attacker who took over admin via initializer) calls `unlistVesting` on any active listing. 2) The penalty branch is skipped because `msg.sender == s2Admin`. 3) `IVestingManager.unlistVesting` is called with `listing.seller` as the recipient, but if `marketplaceSetting` was swapped to a malicious setting, the vesting manager address is attacker-controlled and can redirect tokens.
hypotheses.impact: Sellers lose listing control; combined with setting swap, tokens can be redirected to attacker.
hypotheses.recommendation: Require seller consent for admin-initiated unlisting, or at minimum enforce the penalty and route tokens only to the original seller via a trusted manager.

hypotheses.title: Reentrancy in _createVesting via token transferFrom
hypotheses.description: `_createVesting` writes the `_vestings[_beneficiary]` struct and then, when `!_isInternal`, calls `token.safeTransferFrom(tokenIssuer, address(this), _totalAmount)`. If the vested token has a callback, the tokenIssuer (or a hook) can reenter `createVesting`/`transferVesting` and manipulate `_vestings` state before the outer call's transfer settles, or cause the outer transfer to fail after state was already written.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker controls a hook-capable vested token (or the tokenIssuer is a contract with a callback). 2) Attacker triggers `createVesting`; during `safeTransferFrom` the token reenters `transferVesting` to move the just-created vesting to another address, or reenters `createVesting` to double-count. 3) State written by the outer call is inconsistent with the actual token balance held.
hypotheses.impact: Vesting accounting (`totalAmount`, `releaseRate`) can be inflated relative to tokens actually held, allowing beneficiaries to claim more than deposited and draining the contract.
hypotheses.recommendation: Perform the `safeTransferFrom` before writing `_vestings` state, or add a `nonReentrant` guard to all state-mutating vesting functions.

hypotheses.title: Front-running listVesting to manipulate listing price
hypotheses.description: `listVesting` records `listTime = block.timestamp` and the listing becomes immediately purchasable. A buyer observing a pending `listVesting` transaction in the mempool can front-run it with a `spotPurchase` only after it lands, but more importantly, a seller can front-run a buyer's `spotPurchase` by calling `unlistVesting` (if past `minListingDuration`) or by listing a competing listing at a better price in the same block, sandwiching the buyer's purchase.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Buyer submits `spotPurchase` for a listing. 2) Seller (or a competing seller) observes the pending tx and submits a higher-gas `unlistVesting` or a new `listVesting` at a worse price in the same block. 3) Buyer's tx executes against the manipulated state (listing delisted or price changed), causing revert or worse execution.
hypotheses.impact: Buyers can be forced to pay a worse price or have their purchase reverted after paying gas; sellers can grief buyers by delisting at the last moment.
hypotheses.recommendation: Require a minimum delay between listing creation and first purchase, or use a commit-reveal / signed-order scheme for purchases.

hypotheses.title: Griefing via SINGLE-listing front-run blocks any other buyer forever
hypotheses.description: For SINGLE listings, `_validatePurchase` requires `_amount == listing.total`. Once any buyer executes, `listing.status` becomes SOLDOUT. A malicious buyer can purchase immediately at listing creation, but the more dangerous griefing vector is that a buyer can cause `_handleTransfers` to revert (e.g., via referral accounting where `buyerFeeTotal - (baseAmount*bfee*referralFee)/(BASE*BASE)` underflows if referralFee > BASE) with `_referral != 0`, forcing every subsequent transaction to revert only when the same referral path is used. However, the referral-path underflow bricks only those calls, not the listing.
hypotheses.attackPath: N/A — the true griefing is that `spotPurchase` sends tokens to `listing.seller` via `safeTransfer` and to `feeCollector`; if `feeCollector` is a contract that reverts on receipt, all purchases revert, permanently locking the listing and preventing both purchase and (since tokens went into manager) recovery.
hypotheses.impact: Listing becomes unpurchasable; seller cannot recover remaining balance without admin intervention.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use pull-payments for fee collection or verify `feeCollector` cannot revert on ERC20 receive.

hypotheses.title: createVestings array loop unbounded — admin griefing/OOG lockout
hypotheses.description: `createVestings` loops over caller-supplied arrays calling `_createVesting` each iteration, which performs a `safeTransferFrom` and storage writes per element. A tokenIssuer/manager/deployer caller can submit an enormous array (fills block gas) causing the transaction to revert. While the caller is trusted, the equivalent `WhitelistDeployer.deployWhitelist` is called by any seller in `listVesting`, and `setMaxWhitelist`/whitelist joining are loop-free but the `createVestings` path is restricted. The bigger practical issue: `SecondSwap_VestingDeployer.createVestings` loops again to emit events after the inner loop, doubling gas and risking OOG for moderately-sized arrays.
hypotheses.attackPath: Trusted role only; no untrusted external griefing path found for this specific loop.
hypotheses.impact: Batch vesting creation fails at scale; caller can split into multiple txs.
hypotheses.recommendation: Cap batch size or accept chunked input.

hypotheses.title: completePurchase trusts marketplace caller without verifying payment
hypotheses.description: `completePurchase` is gated only by `onlyMarketplace` and unconditionally credits `allocations[buyer][vesting].bought += amount` and transfers vesting tokens to the buyer. It does not verify that the marketplace actually received payment, nor that the listing exists or that `amount` matches a real purchase. If the marketplace address is ever set to a contract that can be called by an untrusted actor (e.g., via a malicious or upgradeable marketplace), or if the marketplace has any path that calls `completePurchase` without corresponding payment, the buyer receives vesting for free.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker identifies any code path in the marketplace (or a future upgrade) that calls `completePurchase` without a matching `safeTransferFrom` of payment. 2) Attacker triggers that path with a large `amount`. 3) Manager credits `bought` and transfers vesting tokens to attacker. 4) Attacker claims the vesting and sells the tokens, draining the vesting pool.
hypotheses.impact: Free acquisition of vested tokens; vesting pool drained; other beneficiaries unable to claim.
hypotheses.recommendation: Have the marketplace pass a payment proof (e.g., amount paid and currency) and verify it in `completePurchase`, or restrict `completePurchase` to a single audited marketplace path with reentrancy-safe payment ordering.
